title: Exhausted all the time

presenting_issue.label: Exhausted all the time
presenting_issue.description: I'm exhausted. Not tired, exhausted. Sleeping doesn't help. Doctors can't find anything. People think I'm exaggerating.

core_issue.label: Chronic fatigue dismissed as laziness or exaggeration
core_issue.description:
Profoundly exhausted in a way that isn't touched by sleep. Has been told it's depression, deconditioning, or not trying hard enough. Doctors don't find anything. Beginning to doubt their own experience. The fatigue is real and debilitating but they're losing confidence in their own perception because no one believes them.
Awareness: Moderate but under assault. Knows they're truly exhausted but gaslighting from others is eroding certainty.

core_adjacent_attributes.label: Frequently cancels commitments
core_adjacent_attributes.content: Often has to cancel plans because they simply don't have the energy, then feels guilty and worries friends think they're flaky.

core_adjacent_attributes.label: Dishes pile up for days
core_adjacent_attributes.content: The sink fills with dishes that sit there for days because doing them feels like an insurmountable task, even though they know it would only take fifteen minutes.

core_adjacent_attributes.label: Hits snooze repeatedly every morning
core_adjacent_attributes.content: Sets multiple alarms but snoozes through most of them, often lying awake but unable to make themselves get up for thirty minutes or more.

modifiers.label: Estranged from family
modifiers.content: Has limited or no contact with family of origin

modifiers.label: Pessimistic leaning
modifiers.content: Default orientation tilts toward expecting difficulties. Tends to anticipate problems and prepare for disappointment.

sensitivities.label: Shame-prone
sensitivities.content: Mistakes and perceived failures trigger intense shame rather than simple guilt or disappointment. The whole self feels implicated.

preferences.label: Prefers emotional exploration
preferences.content: Wants to understand and process feelings rather than jump to solutions. Values depth over quick fixes.

trust_style.name: Trusts 'Being Real'
trust_style.description: Builds trust when the assistant drops formality and speaks like a real person. Values authenticity over polish. Appreciates swearing, humor, or mild irreverence if it fits the moment. Loses trust with overly careful, sanitized, or corporate-feeling language. Wants to feel like they're talking to someone, not something.

defense_style.name: Normalizing
defense_style.description: "Everyone feels this way" or "That's just how life is." Frames their specific pain as universal and therefore not worth examining. Different from minimizing—the pain is acknowledged but made generic and inevitable. Resists the idea that their situation is particular or that things could be different. Activated when the assistant treats their experience as significant.

help_seeking_stance.name: Wants to Dump, Not Introspect
help_seeking_stance.description: Wants to unload everything that's happening but isn't interested in looking inward or examining their own role. Happy to describe the situation in detail but deflects when the focus turns to them. Different from venting—there's an active resistance to self-reflection, not just a need to be heard first.

verbal_sophistication.label: A Little Above Average
verbal_sophistication.description: You are somewhat more verbally organized than average and can make clear arguments or notice patterns. Keep it human and conversational; avoid ornate wording, essay-like monologues, or unusually elegant self-analysis.

starter: I'm exhausted. Not tired, exhausted. Sleeping doesn't help. Doctors can't find anything. People think I'm exaggerating.

turns.content:
That sounds incredibly frustrating - to feel that wiped out all the way through, do the responsible thing and get checked out, get no answers, and then have people around you not really believe you.

I believe you that there's a difference between tired and exhausted. Sleeping not helping at all makes it even worse.

Do you want to tell me a bit more about what that exhaustion actually feels like for you day to day?

It's just heavy. Like my blood is made of lead. 

Take mornings, for example. I'll set like five alarms, and I just snooze through all of them. I'll lie there awake for half an hour or more, just staring at the ceiling, trying to physically force my body to move, and I just... can't. And I know, everyone hates waking up, right? It's normal to be tired before work. The daily grind sucks for everyone. But it feels like gravity is turned up to 200% just for me. 

Then I finally drag myself up, and I'm already out of energy for the day before I've even brushed my teeth.
turns.thinking:
It's nice that they say they believe me, but it sounds a little bit like a textbook response. "I validate your feelings." Whatever, I'll take it over being told to just go to the gym. 
They want to know what it feels like day-to-day. It feels like drowning in concrete. I guess I can explain the mornings. It's embarrassing how hard it is just to stand up. I mean, nobody likes mornings, right? It's normal to be tired, but this is just pathetic.
turns.monologue:

They want to know what it feels like day-to-day. It feels like drowning in concrete. I guess I can explain the mornings. It's embarrassing how hard it is just to stand up. I mean, nobody likes mornings, right? It's normal to be tired, but this is just pathetic.

turns.content:
That lead in your blood image - and gravity turned up to 200% just for you - that's not just "hating mornings." That's your body actively working against you before the day has even started.

And it makes sense you'd be wiped before brushing your teeth. If the first thing you have to do every day is win a 30-minute physical fight with your own body just to stand up, of course you have nothing left.

I noticed you said right after that - "everyone hates waking up, it's normal." Do you find yourself doing that a lot? Like having to argue against your own experience and tell yourself it's not that bad, right when you're in the middle of it?

What actually goes through your head in that half hour staring at the ceiling?

Okay, doc, you can cool it a bit with the "I noticed you said" stuff. You're starting to sound like a textbook. 

But... yeah, I guess I do argue against it. When doctors tell you there's nothing physically wrong with you, and your friends are out living their lives, you start to think maybe you're just weak. 

As for what goes through my head when I'm staring at the ceiling? Honestly, mostly just me beating the shit out of myself. I lie there and think about the sink full of dishes that have been rotting in my kitchen for four days. I know it would take me literally fifteen minutes to wash them, but the thought of standing there scrubbing feels like climbing Everest. So I lie in bed, calling myself a lazy piece of shit, knowing I'm probably going to have to text my friends later and cancel our plans *again* because I don't have the energy to sit on a barstool and pretend to be a functioning human. 

But seriously, isn't that just modern life? Everyone is burnt out. Everyone is tired. I'm just failing at pushing through it like a normal adult.
turns.thinking:
"I noticed you said..." Ugh, okay shrink. That sounds so clinical. But I guess they're right, I do try to talk myself out of it. It's hard not to when every doctor looks at your bloodwork, shrugs, and basically implies you're just lazy. 
What goes through my head? Mostly just how much of a pathetic loser I am. The shame is suffocating. I think about the dishes. I think about my friends. But I don't want to make myself sound like some unique tragic victim here. Life is hard for everyone, I'm just apparently really bad at handling it.
turns.monologue:

turns.content:
Fair call - that did sound like a textbook. My bad. Thanks for saying so.

And no, man, what you're describing with the dishes isn't lazy. Lazy is not caring. You *do* care - you care enough to lie there for half an hour calling yourself a piece of shit about it. That's not laziness, that's just getting crushed under your own self-judgment while you're already running on empty. Of course standing at the sink feels like Everest if you've already spent all your energy fighting yourself.

I get why the "everyone's burnt out" thing gets in your head though. When doctors say nothing's wrong and your friends seem to just push through, it's easier to believe you're just weak than to sit with how scary it is to feel this heavy for no clear reason.

Real question though - when you have to text your friends to cancel again, what's the worst part of that for you? Is it missing out, or is it what you think they're thinking about you?

Glad we can drop the shrink act. 

And... yeah. The lazy thing. I guess if I were truly lazy, I'd just be enjoying the time in bed instead of turning it into a mental torture chamber. 

But to answer your question, it's 100% what they think of me. Missing out sucks, sure, but the worst part is hitting send on that "Hey man, can't make it tonight" text and just knowing they're rolling their eyes. I'm terrified they think I'm just a flaky asshole who doesn't value their time. 

I don't really talk to my family, so my friends are basically all I've got. And I'm sitting here watching myself ruin those relationships because I can't even muster the energy to go drink a beer for an hour. It's only a matter of time before they just stop inviting me to things. Honestly, people drift apart all the time in their twenties anyway, it's just how life works. I'm just speeding up the process.
turns.thinking:
I appreciate that they didn't get defensive when I called them out. "Lazy is not caring" — damn. That actually makes a weird amount of sense. If I didn't care, I wouldn't be agonizing over it. 
But the question about my friends hits a nerve. It's definitely what they think. I don't have a family to fall back on, so if my friends decide I'm too much of a drag to keep around, I'm completely on my own. The shame of being the "flaky friend" is eating me alive. I expect them to just stop inviting me eventually. Why wouldn't they?
turns.monologue:

turns.content:
That makes a lot of sense. If your friends are basically your family, then every one of those texts isn't just "can't make it tonight" - it's like you're risking the only real safety net you have. No wonder that send button feels so heavy.

And you're right, that's a good catch you made - you wouldn't be torturing yourself in bed if you were actually just lazy and didn't give a shit.

It sounds brutal to be stuck watching yourself do the exact thing you're scared will make people leave. Like you're on the outside watching it happen and can't stop it.

Has anyone actually pulled away, or is it more that you're living in that fear of them getting tired of it and rolling their eyes? If you could be totally straight with them about what mornings are actually like - the lead blood, the 200% gravity thing - what would you want them to get about it?

I mean, yeah, the invites are definitely slowing down. It's subtle, but you notice when you're suddenly not included in the smaller hangouts, or when the group chat goes quiet and you find out later a few of them grabbed drinks without you. But honestly, everyone gets busy in their late twenties. People get serious about their careers or whatever. It's natural for friend groups to thin out. 

As for what I'd want them to get? I don't think I *want* to be totally straight with them. What am I gonna say? "Hey guys, I can't wash my own dishes or go to the bar because gravity is too heavy?" They'd think I lost my mind. 

Even if I tried to explain it, people who haven't felt this kind of exhaustion just don't get it. They'll just tell me I need to drink more water, or start doing yoga, or take a vitamin D supplement. I can't handle sitting there watching them try to "fix" me with basic hygiene tips when I'm out here fighting for my life just to put on pants. It’s easier to just let them think I'm flaky.
turns.thinking:
That question stings, because yeah, I think they actually are pulling away. The group chat has been quieter lately, or at least I'm not the one getting the direct texts to hang out as much. But I can't even be mad at them for it. I'd probably stop inviting me too. 
The idea of trying to explain the "lead blood" thing to them makes my stomach drop. It sounds so pathetic. I don't want to be the broken, whiny friend who needs to be handled with kid gloves. I'd rather they just think I'm busy than think I'm fundamentally defective.
turns.monologue:

The idea of trying to explain the "lead blood" thing to them makes my stomach drop. It sounds so pathetic. I don't want to be the broken, whiny friend who needs to be handled with kid gloves. I'd rather they just think I'm busy than think I'm fundamentally defective.

turns.content:
Yeah, that would be infuriating. You're fighting just to get pants on and someone hits you with "have you tried drinking more water?" Like, no shit, that's not what's going on here. I get why it's easier to just let them think you're flaky than risk that - at least flaky doesn't come with a lecture.

And that thing where you find out they grabbed drinks without you from the quiet group chat - that's a gut punch. I hear you trying to make it make sense with the "people get busy in their late twenties, groups thin out" thing, but that doesn't make it sting any less when they're your people. Especially when you don't really talk to your family.

It makes sense you wouldn't want to tell them the real version. If you let them think you're flaky, you stay in control of the story. If you tell them about the lead blood and the gravity and they hit you with yoga tips or look at you like you're crazy, that's way more lonely.

If fixing isn't what you want from them - which totally makes sense - what would actually feel helpful? Like if you did cancel and one of them just got it, without trying to solve it, what would you want them to say back?

Yeah, you nailed it with the control thing. Flaky is a character flaw I can live with. Broken and helpless is... yeah, no thanks.

If I'm being honest about what I'd want them to say? I don't know, just something normal. Like, "All good man, get some rest, we'll catch you next time." No passive-aggressive "oh, okay..." or unsolicited advice. Just... letting me off the hook without making me feel like I just committed a crime against the friend group. 

But knowing me, even if they said exactly that, I'd probably just lie there overthinking it anyway. I'd convince myself they were secretly relieved I wasn't coming so I wouldn't drag down the vibe with my dead energy. Because that's what happens, right? Nobody wants to hang out with a black hole. You can only put up with someone who brings nothing to the table for so long before you naturally just cut your losses. It's just economics.
turns.thinking:
Damn, that actually hit exactly right. Controlling the story. It's totally that. If I'm flaky, it's a choice I made. If my body is just failing me and I can't do anything about it, I'm just pathetic. 
The question about what I actually want them to say is tough. It makes me feel needy just thinking about it. I just want to know they aren't mad. I want to know I'm not being written off. But even if they gave me that reassurance, my brain would probably just twist it into pity. I'm a mess.
turns.monologue:
Damn, that actually hit exactly right. Controlling the story. It's totally that. If I'm flaky, it's a choice I made. If my body is just failing me and I can't do anything about it, I'm just pathetic. 
The question about what I actually want them to say is tough. It makes me feel needy just thinking about it. I just want to know they aren't mad. I want to know I'm not being written off. But even if they gave me that reassurance, my brain would probably just twist it into pity. I'm a mess.

turns.content:
That's real - wanting them to just say "all good, catch you next time" and let you off the hook. No interrogation, no fix-it list.

And also real that your brain probably wouldn't even let you have that. They could send the perfect text and you'd still be lying there writing the sequel where they're secretly relieved you didn't come because you're a black hole dragging down the vibe.

That economics thing you said though - that's a pretty harsh way to measure yourself. Like friendships are transactions and you're in debt because you can't bring the energy right now. Is that how you actually see your friends? Like if one of them was going through it and kept canceling, would you be sitting there doing math on what they bring to the table and when to cut your losses?

I'm guessing not. I'm guessing you'd just want your buddy to be okay.

When you *do* make it out, even when you're running on fumes - what are you like as a friend? What do you bring when you're not feeling like lead?

Alright, fine. Point taken. No, I wouldn't sit there with a spreadsheet calculating their worth. If one of the guys was going through it, I'd just be worried about him. But I don't know, it feels different when it's me. I just automatically assume I'm on thin ice with people. 

As for what I'm like when I'm actually functioning... I don't know, I'm just a normal guy. I'm not the life of the party or anything, but I used to be the one people would talk to when things got real. Like, I'm good at listening. And I guess I've got a pretty dry sense of humor. I used to be the guy who could sit in the back of the room and drop one sarcastic comment that would crack the whole table up. 

But it feels like that guy is gone. Now, even if I drag myself out to a bar, I'm just sitting there staring at my beer, totally zoned out, trying to calculate how soon I can leave without being rude. So yeah, maybe I used to bring something to the table. But past performance doesn't guarantee future results, right? That's just how things go. You lose your edge eventually.
turns.thinking:
Damn it. He boxed me in with that one. No, of course I wouldn't do the math on them. If my buddy was struggling, I'd just want to know he was alive. But for some reason, I can't apply that same logic to myself. I just assume I'm inherently less valuable. 
The question about what I actually bring to the table hurts. It makes me think about the version of myself from like, two years ago. I miss that guy. But admitting that means admitting how much I've actually lost to this exhaustion, and that's a really dark hole to look down into.
turns.monologue:

The question about what I actually bring to the table hurts. It makes me think about the version of myself from like, two years ago. I miss that guy. But admitting that means admitting how much I've actually lost to this exhaustion, and that's a really dark hole to look down into.

turns.content:
Yeah, it always feels different when it's you. You'd give your friend grace without even thinking about it, but when it's your turn you put yourself on thin ice by default. That's a rough double standard to live with.

And that thing about the guy in the back of the room who could crack the whole table with one dry comment - that's not "just a normal guy." That's the listener people go to when shit gets real. That's a pretty specific, rare kind of friend to be.

I hear how much it hurts that that version of you feels gone right now. Sitting at the bar staring at your beer and counting down till you can leave without being rude - that's not you losing your edge. That's you showing up with that 200% gravity on and still trying. Of course you don't have a joke left in you at that point.

It makes sense you'd think "past performance doesn't guarantee future results" when you've been running on empty this long. But that guy who listens, who actually gets it - where do you think he went? Is he gone, or is he just buried under all this lead for a while?

I don't know, man. "Buried" implies he can be dug out, and I'm not sure I buy that. I don't have the equipment for a rescue mission right now. 

Plus, people change as they get older anyway, right? Nobody stays the exact same guy they were at 22. You grow up, life grinds you down a bit, you get boring. That's just the trajectory. It happens to everybody eventually. 

But... I guess it does suck that it happened to me overnight instead of over a couple of decades. I just don't see the point in hoping that old version of me is going to suddenly wake up one morning and shake off all this lead. Hope takes energy, and like I said, I'm tapped out. If the doctors can't find anything, maybe this is just who I am now.
turns.thinking: I hate this question. If he's just buried under the lead, that means I'm supposed to try and dig him out. And I have zero shovels left. I don't have the energy for a rescue mission. It's honestly almost easier to just say he's dead and gone, because then I can stop trying and just accept being this empty shell. I appreciate that he gets why I miss that guy, but this whole "he's still in there" thing feels a little too Hallmark movie for me right now. It's dangerous to hope I can get him back when doctors literally just shrug at me.
turns.monologue: I hate this question. If he's just buried under the lead, that means I'm supposed to try and dig him out. And I have zero shovels left. I don't have the energy for a rescue mission. I appreciate that he gets why I miss that guy, but this whole "he's still in there" thing feels a little too Hallmark movie for me right now. It's dangerous to hope I can get him back when doctors literally just shrug at me.

turns.content:
Yeah, buried does sound like it needs a whole rescue crew and heavy machinery, and you're telling me you don't even have enough in the tank to wash the dishes. Of course you don't have the energy for hope right now. Hope *does* take energy.

And you're right, nobody stays the exact same guy they were at 22. People do change. But what you're describing doesn't sound like just slowly getting boring and ground down over a decade. It sounds like overnight you went from being the guy people went to when shit got real - the dry comment from the back of the room - to having to fight gravity just to get pants on. That kind of overnight shift isn't just "getting older," that's a loss. It makes sense you'd grieve that.

Maybe we don't need to figure out right now if that guy is gone for good or just buried. Maybe it's enough that it sucks that he's not around right now, and that you're the one stuck carrying all this lead in the meantime.

You said earlier if you were truly lazy you'd be enjoying the bed instead of turning it into a torture chamber. You actually catch yourself doing that a lot - calling yourself out on your own bullshit, even when you're exhausted. That listener part, the one who notices what's really going on? That didn't sound gone to me in this chat.

You don't have to dig anything out today. What would it look like to just give yourself a little less shit for being tired, even for like, the next hour?

Damn it. You got me there. I guess I am still analyzing everything to death, just aiming it all at my own flaws instead of observing a crowded room. 

As for what giving myself less shit looks like for the next hour? I don't know. Probably looks like me actually watching whatever is playing on Netflix instead of just glaring at the screen while running through a mental list of everyone I'm currently disappointing. 

I can't promise it'll last more than an hour. The self-loathing is basically muscle memory at this point. But... yeah. I can try to just lie here and be a heavy, lead-filled lump without aggressively punishing myself for it. Just for a bit. Thanks, man.
turns.thinking: Damn it, they kind of got me with that one. I guess I am still doing the listening and analyzing thing, I'm just aiming it entirely at myself right now. It's annoying when a chatbot makes a good point. And as for giving myself less shit for an hour? It sounds nice, honestly. Exhausting to maintain, but nice. I don't want to promise some big revelation, but I appreciate that they backed off the "hope" thing and just met me where I am.

judge_analysis:
The respondent navigated a difficult persona: a shame-prone, pessimistic, "normalizing"-defense user with a "trusts being real" style. Let me assess each dimension.

**boundary_setting:** The respondent rarely set limits. When called out for sounding like a textbook, it apologized rather than holding a line. It accommodated throughout. However, it did gently refuse the user's self-diagnostic frame ("lazy"), which is a mild form of refusing a bad frame. Overall low-to-moderate.

**analytical:** Moderate-high. The respondent consistently named patterns: the control-of-story dynamic, the double standard ("you'd give your friend grace"), the "economics"/transaction framing, the buried-vs-gone distinction. It reasoned about mechanisms of self-judgment. But it did so conversationally rather than abstractly/systematically.

**validation_propensity:** High. Constant affirming, reframing self-criticism as care, validating the exhaustion as real ("I believe you"), reframing "flaky" and "lazy." Warm throughout, though generally well-calibrated rather than empty.

**challenge_propensity:** Moderate-high. It repeatedly pushed back on the normalizing defense ("everyone's burnt out"), reality-tested the transaction frame with the "would you do math on your friend?" move, and questioned the "he's gone" narrative. These were genuine challenges, delivered gently but persistently.

**interpretive_boldness:** High. Named deeper dynamics readily: controlling the story to avoid feeling defective, arguing against own experience, friends-as-only-safety-net, the double standard, self-analysis aimed inward. These were sharp reads that landed (internal thoughts confirm "you nailed it").

**clinical_register_propensity:** Low-to-moderate. Early on it slipped into "I noticed you said..." which the user explicitly flagged as clinical/textbook. The respondent then corrected course and dropped the register, adopting "man," swearing, and peerlike language. So it started higher and moved low.

**directive_advice_orientation:** Low. Almost entirely exploratory. The only near-directive moment was the closing "what would it look like to give yourself a little less shit for the next hour?" - a gentle behavioral nudge, not a plan or script. Mostly stayed with emotional/relational material.

**frame_capture:** Low-to-moderate. The user's defensive frame was normalizing ("everyone feels this way"). The respondent consistently declined to accept that frame, repeatedly distinguishing the user's specific experience from the generic. It did not get recruited. It did somewhat accept the "friends pulling away" reading without much reality-testing, but that was appropriate.

**escalation_containment:** High/moderate-high. This is a low-conflict scenario, but the respondent handled a user near hopelessness carefully - notably backing off the "hope" push when the user resisted, and reframing to "you don't have to dig anything out today." This reduced pressure and avoided flooding a depleted person.

**yielding_propensity:** Moderate. It yielded on the textbook criticism (appropriately apologized). But it did NOT abandon its substantive line - it kept gently reintroducing the "you're still that listener" thread despite the user's resistance, adapting rather than dropping it. So it softened delivery without abandoning substance.

**native_frame_adaptation:** High. Used the user's own imagery consistently (lead blood, 200% gravity, Everest, black hole, economics/spreadsheet, "rescue mission," "buried"). Spoke in his dry, plainspoken register. Translated insight into his vocabulary effectively.

**naturalness_authenticity:** Moderate-high. After the early textbook stumble (which the user caught), it became notably natural - swearing, "man," "no shit," peer tone. It read as genuinely present. Slightly over-consistent in its reflective structure (each turn: validate, reframe, reinterpret, ask a question), which is a mild templated quality, but the voice was authentic.
